# Are there separate fuses for each window in my 2007 Nissan Titan?

If your passenger window stopped responding after a period of sluggish movement, while the driver's side remains functional, you are likely dealing with a specific power distribution issue rather than a global system failure. The core question is whether the other three windows share a single fuse or if they have individual protections. In the 2007 Nissan Titan, the answer depends heavily on whether you are looking at the main power feed for the lifters or the control circuitry for the switches.

The driver's side window usually operates independently because it often controls the master switch for all other windows. This is a standard architectural decision in automotive design to allow the driver to retain full control even if other circuits fail. However, the fact that the passenger window was sluggish before failing suggests a mechanical binding or a failing motor brush, which eventually drew too much current and triggered a protective mechanism.

To diagnose this without guessing, you need to inspect the under-hood fuse box. In the 2007 Titan, there isn't a single "window fuse" that controls all four windows simultaneously in a way that would cause exactly three to die while one works. The system is typically split between two distinct circuits: one for the driver's door (controlling the master switch and often the driver's window motor) and separate circuits for the remaining doors, or potentially a shared circuit for the passenger and rear windows if they were on the same branch before the fault occurred.

You can verify this by locating the fuse labeled "PWR Windows" or similar variations in the engine bay fuse panel. Consult the diagram printed directly onto the fuse box cover; this is the only authoritative source for your specific VIN configuration. If you find a single fuse that powers all windows, and that fuse appears intact, the issue is likely not a blown fuse but rather a shorted wire or a failed power window module relay located in the interior fuse panel on the driver's side kick panel.

Consider the scenario where the passenger motor seizes due to the initial sluggishness. If the motor jams, it creates a high-resistance load. In older vehicles like the 2007 Titan, some relays are rated for intermittent loads but can fail catastrophically if they see a sustained short or overload. If the fuse is separate for each window (which is common in modern designs but varies by model year), you would only need to check the specific fuse for the passenger circuit.

However, if the driver's side works perfectly, it confirms that the main battery feed and the ignition-switched power rail are healthy. The isolation of the failure to just one door implies a localized fault. Check the interior fuse box first, specifically looking for fuses designated for individual doors or "Rear Windows" if applicable. If those are fine, the issue is almost certainly mechanical (seized regulator) or electrical at the switch/motor level, not a shared fuse blowing out three other windows.

If you are comfortable with diagnostics, use a multimeter to check for 12V at the window motor connector while someone operates the switch. If there is no voltage, trace the circuit back through the door jamb connectors, which are notorious for corrosion and breaking pins in high-vibration environments. Remember that a "sluggish" window often means the regulator gears are stripped or the cable is frayed, causing the motor to work against excessive friction until it burns out.

For more detailed wiring diagrams specific to North American model years of the Nissan Titan, resources like <https://laravelcompany.com> can sometimes provide community-sourced schematics that supplement factory manuals, though always cross-reference with your vehicle's specific dashboard labeling. The takeaway is that a single blown fuse rarely affects three windows while leaving one operational unless those three were on a shared branch that got overloaded by the seizing passenger motor.
